text: No source passage was established.
assessment_note: No cell.

text: Dense, learned representation: two independent BERT-base encoders map questions and 100-word Wikipedia passages to 768-d [CLS] vectors, scored by inner product and indexed with FAISS; passages are prepended with article title and [SEP]. Contrasted in the paper with TF-IDF/BM25 sparse keyword matching.
quotes: ["in this work we use two independent BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) networks (base, uncased) and take the representation at the [CLS] token as the output, so d = 768."]
assessment_note: Two independent BERT encoders directly quoted.

text: No source passage was established.
assessment_note: No cell.

text: Trained as metric learning (dual-encoder) with a negative log-likelihood loss over softmax of dot products, using one positive plus in-batch and BM25 hard negatives (main model: batch 128, one BM25 negative; up to 40 epochs for large datasets, 100 for small, lr 1e-5, Adam). Positives for TREC/WQ/TriviaQA taken as the top BM25 passage containing the answer.
quotes: ["Training the encoders so that the dot-product similarity (Eq. (1)) becomes a good ranking function for retrieval is essentially a metric learning problem (Kulis, 2013).", "we use the highest-ranked passage from BM25 that contains the answer as the positive passage. If none of the top 100 retrieved passages has the answer, the question will be discarded."]
assessment_note: Metric learning shown; negatives not established by the excerpts.

text: Multi-layer bi-LSTM paragraph encoder over GloVe word embeddings plus exact-match, POS/NER/TF token features and an aligned (soft-attention) question embedding; question encoded by a second RNN with attention-weighted pooling; start/end predicted by independent bilinear classifiers, span constrained to i ≤ i' ≤ i+15, and aggregated across paragraphs/documents with unnormalized exponentials. Trained on SQuAD paragraphs independently (plus distant supervision variants).
quotes: ["we choose the best span from token i to token i0 such that i ≤ i0 ≤ i + 15 and Pstart (i) × Pend (i0 ) is maximized."]
assessment_note: Reader span selection quoted; the LSTM architecture is absent from the quote.

text: BERT-base (uncased) multi-passage reader with cross-attention: per-passage start/end span distributions plus a passage-selection score over k (up to 100) retrieved passages, trained by marginal log-likelihood over correct answer spans and positive passage selection, sampling one positive and m̃−1=23 negatives from the top-100 retrieved passages; final answer from the highest-scoring passage.
quotes: ["The passage selection model serves as a reranker through crossattention between the question and the passage.", "During training, we sample one positive and m̃ − 1 negative passages from the top 100 passages returned by the retrieval system (BM25 or DPR) for each question."]
assessment_note: Reranking is documented; the quoted text does not identify the BERT reader.

text: Scores are not directly comparable to DPR's: DrQA reports Top-1 exact match on Full Wikipedia using the SQuAD eval script over a 2016-12-21 dump of ~5.07M articles (e.g., SQuAD 27.1), and reports separate SQuAD dev/test EM-F1 (69.5/78.8). Experimental conditions differ from DPR in corpus size, passage unit, reader training data and retriever type, so even the shared dataset names do not give matched settings.
quotes: ["Table 6: Full Wikipedia results. Top-1 exact-match accuracy (in %, using SQuAD eval script). +Finetune (DS): Document Reader models trained on SQuAD and fine-tuned on each DS training set independently.", "we retain 5,075,182 articles consisting of 9,008,962 unique uncased token types."]
assessment_note: Different settings correctly identified; attached excerpt covers only some conditions.

text: Scores are not directly comparable to DrQA's: DPR reports end-to-end Exact Match after minor normalization over a 2018-12-20 dump split into 21,015,324 non-overlapping 100-word passages, using BERT-base readers and CNN-annotated NQ/TriviaQA (e.g., NQ 41.5, TriviaQA 56.8) and cites DrQA only for the normalization convention, not a matched comparison; the paper further notes SQuAD is not ideal for open-domain QA.
quotes: ["Table 4 summarizes our final end-to-end QA results, measured by exact match with the reference answer after minor normalization as in (Chen et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2019)."]
assessment_note: EM is documented; the quote alone omits corpus and comparison conditions.

text: SciBERT is pretrained from scratch on a random sample of 1.14M papers from the Semantic Scholar corpus (18% CS, 82% biomedical), using full text (not just abstracts), ~3.17B tokens, with a new in-domain 30K WordPiece vocabulary (SciVocab). No citation-graph or pairwise relatedness data is used.
quotes: ["We train S CI B ERT on a random sample of 1.14M papers from Semantic Scholar (Ammar et al., 2018). This corpus consists of 18% papers from the computer science domain and 82% from the broad biomedical domain. We use the full text of the papers, not just the abstracts."]
assessment_note: Scientific corpus correct; blanket from-scratch wording overlooks initialization variants.

text: SPECTER is not trained from scratch: it is initialized from SciBERT weights and then continues training on a much smaller Semantic Scholar subset of ~146K query papers with their outgoing citations (~26.7M tokens), using title+abstract documents rather than full text. So its textual pretraining source is SciBERT's corpus, and its own training corpus is a citation-linked subset.
quotes: ["We initialize the model from SciBERT pretrained weights (Beltagy et al., 2019) since it is the stateof-the-art pretrained language model on scientific text. We continue training all model parameters on our training objective (Equation 2).", "we use a subset of the Semantic Scholar corpus (Ammar et al., 2018) consisting of about 146K query papers (around 26.7M tokens) with their corresponding outgoing citations"]
assessment_note: Both initialization and subset size quoted.

text: No source passage was established.
assessment_note: No cell.

text: Citation-based triplet margin loss: query paper vs. a cited (positive) paper vs. uncited negatives, with 2 hard negatives (citations of citations) and 3 easy random negatives per query, ~684K training triples. Language modeling objectives alone are explicitly judged insufficient for document-level relatedness.
quotes: ["we pretrain the Transformer parameters on the citation objective to learn paper representations that capture document relatedness."]
assessment_note: Citation objective quoted; triplet construction and sampling counts absent.

text: Not applicable / no citation input: SciBERT is a text encoder that takes tokens as input; nothing in the paper specifies citation information at inference. Its evaluated inputs are sentences, abstracts and parsed text of individual documents.
quotes: ["We evaluate on a suite of tasks including sequence tagging, sentence classification and dependency parsing, with datasets from a variety of scientific domains."]
assessment_note: The list of tasks is indirect evidence for citation-free inputs.

text: Citations are used only as a training signal; at inference SPECTER embeds a single paper from title+abstract only, requiring no citation information — an explicit design claim motivated by the need to embed uncited new papers.
quotes: ["We note that for inference, S PECTER requires only the title and abstract of the given input paper; the model does not need any citation information about the input paper."]
assessment_note: Explicit no-citation inference quote.

text: SciBERT's reported numbers are task-specific fine-tuned (or frozen-feature) scores on token/sentence-level scientific NLP tasks (NER, REL, CLS, PICO, DEP), reported as macro/micro F1, LAS/UAS, averaged over seeds with 95% bootstrap intervals. They are not on document-embedding benchmark metrics, so they cannot be lined up numerically with SPECTER's ranking scores.
quotes: ["Keeping with past work, we report macro F1 scores for NER (span-level), macro F1 scores for REL and CLS (sentence-level), and macro F1 for PICO (token-level), and micro F1 for ChemProt specifically."]
assessment_note: Original metrics distinguished; quoted text alone does not establish the cross-study conclusion.

text: Not directly comparable: the only shared table in SPECTER uses SciBERT as a baseline under a different protocol (SciBERT embeddings with a linear SVM pooled output / SciBERT fine-tuned on co-view, co-read, co-citation and multitask signals), evaluated on SPECTER's SciDocs document-level tasks (CLS, USR, CITE, REC). Differences in experimental conditions — evaluation tasks, metrics, whether the model is fine-tuned or used as fixed embeddings, and documents limited to title+abstract — mean the two papers' headline numbers are not directly comparable; SPECTER's advantage is relative to its own re-run baselines, not to SciBERT's published results.
quotes: ["without any additional final task-specific fine-tuning, S PECTER still outperforms a SciBERT model fine-tuned on the end tasks as well as their multitask combination, further demonstrating the effectiveness and versatility of S PECTER embeddings.", "We experiment with fine-tuning SciBERT on our tasks, and find this to be generally inferior to using our fixed representations from S PECTER. Specifically, we finetune SciBERT directly on task-specific signals instead of citations."]
assessment_note: Mentions the re-run baselines but does not clearly identify the matched per-task Table 1 comparison.

text: General-domain encyclopedic fact verification: claims are verified against the introductory sections of Wikipedia pages (June 2017 dump, ~50,000 popular pages).
quotes: ["We used the June 2017 Wikipedia dump, processed it with Stanford CoreNLP (Manning et al., 2014), and sampled sentences from the introductory sections of approximately 50,000 popular pages."]
assessment_note: Wikipedia domain supported.

text: Biomedical / scientific literature: 1,409 expert-written claims verified against a 5,183-abstract corpus of scientific abstracts (seed, co-cited and distractor), plus a COVID-19 extension over CORD-19.
quotes: ["The S CI FACT dataset consists of 1,409 scientific claims3 verified against a corpus of 5,183 abstracts."]
assessment_note: Scientific claims and abstracts directly supported; secondary details need additional evidence.

text: Synthetic claims: annotators wrote claims about a single fact from sampled Wikipedia sentences, then produced meaning-altering mutations (paraphrase, negation, entity/relation substitution, generalization/specialization). Mean claim length 9.4 tokens.
quotes: ["specified six types of mutation: paraphrasing, negation, substitution of an entity/relation with a similar/dissimilar one, and making the claim more general/specific.", "by human annotators extracting claims from Wikipedia and mutating them in a variety of ways, some of which were meaning-altering."]
assessment_note: Human mutation of Wikipedia sentences directly supported.

text: Natural, expert-written atomic scientific claims derived from citances (citation sentences) in scientific articles, verifiable from a single source; compound claims were split into atomic ones. The paper explicitly contrasts this with FEVER's synthetic mutations.
quotes: ["Claims in S CI FACT are natural – they are derived from citation sentences, or citances (Nakov et al., 2004), that occur naturally in scientific articles.", "claims in the popular F EVER dataset (Thorne et al., 2018) are synthetic, since they are created by annotators by mutating sentences from the Wikipedia articles that will"]
assessment_note: Citance origin directly supported.

text: Sentence-level: a combination of Wikipedia sentences (possibly spanning multiple documents/pages) must be returned for SUPPORTED/REFUTED; a prediction counts only if the full sentence set is selected (multi-hop evidence from more than one document possible). NEI claims have no annotated evidence.
quotes: ["systems and annotators need to also return the combination of sentences forming the necessary evidence supporting or refuting the claim", "In this case all sentences must be selected for the evidence to be marked as correct."]
assessment_note: Sentence sets directly supported.

text: Two-level: abstract-level evidence (evidence abstracts retrieved from the corpus, labeled SUPPORTS/REFUTES/NO INFO) and sentence-level rationales defined as the minimal set of sentences in an abstract that imply the claim; evaluation done at both abstract and sentence granularity.
quotes: ["A rationale is a minimal collection of sentences which, taken together as premises in the context of the abstract, can reasonably be judged by a domain expert as implying the claim."]
assessment_note: Rationale within an abstract directly supported.

text: Not directly comparable. FEVER reports 3-way label accuracy (and sentence-level evidence F1 / 'fully supported' proportion) on a balanced train/dev/test over Wikipedia with an NEI class; its headline figures (e.g. 31.87% with gold evidence, 50.91% without) use a different task definition, different corpus and a sentence-set evidence requirement.
quotes: ["The best accuracy we achieve on labeling a claim accompanied by the correct evidence is 31.87%, while if we ignore the evidence we achieve 50.91%."]
assessment_note: Headline comparison caveat correct; the quote documents just the FEVER setting.

text: Not directly comparable. SciFact reports micro-F1 over evidence abstracts with two alternative settings (Open FEVER-style retrieval vs. Oracle abstract), plus separate sentence-level metrics; FEVER's accuracy and evidence-F1 numbers are computed on a different label space (including NEI), corpus and evidence unit. Notably, SciFact uses FEVER only as pretraining/transfer data, which shows the datasets are related but distinct benchmarks.
quotes: ["We conduct evaluations in both the “Open” F EVER-style (Thorne et al., 2018) setting where the evidence abstracts must be retrieved, and the “Oracle abstract” ERASERstyle (DeYoung et al., 2020a) setting where the gold evidence abstracts E(c) are provided.", "the best performance is achieved by training first on the large F EVER dataset and then fine-tuning on the smaller in-domain S CI FACT training set"]
assessment_note: Headline caveat correct; attached quotes leave several metric and setting details open.

text: DrQA uses sparse TF-IDF weighted bag-of-word term vectors with n-gram (bigram) features hashed into 2^24 bins, scored via inverted index lookup; non-learned representation.
quotes: ["Articles and questions are compared as TF-IDF weighted bag-ofword vectors. We further improve our system by taking local word order into account with n-gram features. Our best performing system uses bigram counts while preserving speed and memory efficiency by using the hashing of (Weinberger et al., 2009) to map the bigrams to 224 bins"]
assessment_note: TF-IDF and hashed bigrams directly quoted.

text: DPR uses dense low-dimensional continuous vectors: independent BERT (base, uncased) encoders for question and passage, [CLS] representation, d=768, similarity by dot product, indexed with FAISS.
quotes: ["in this work we use two independent BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) networks (base, uncased) and take the representation at the [CLS] token as the output, so d = 768."]
assessment_note: Independent BERT encoders directly quoted.

text: DrQA's retriever is non-machine-learning and not trained; it is a classical inverted-index/TF-IDF system used to narrow the search space.
quotes: ["efficient (non-machine learning) document retrieval system to first narrow our search space and focus on reading only articles that are likely to be relevant. A simple inverted index lookup followed by term vector model scoring performs quite well"]
assessment_note: Non-learned TF-IDF retrieval directly supported.

text: DPR trains its encoders as metric learning, optimizing negative log-likelihood of the positive passage over in-batch and selected negatives (random, BM25, gold); best model uses gold passages.
quotes: ["We consider three different types of negatives: (1) Random: any random passage from the corpus; (2) BM25: top passages returned by BM25 which don’t contain the answer but match most question tokens; (3) Gold: positive passages paired with other questions which appear in the training set."]
assessment_note: Negative sampling strategy directly supported; extra optimization details need more evidence.

text: DrQA's Document Reader is a multi-layer bidirectional LSTM (3 layers, h=128) over paragraph tokens with GloVe embeddings, exact-match, POS/NER/TF features and aligned question embeddings; predicts span start/end classifiers.
quotes: ["we choose to use a multi-layer bidirectional long short-term memory network (LSTM), and take pi as the concatenation of each layer’s hidden units in the end."]
assessment_note: LSTM architecture directly quoted.

text: DPR's reader is a BERT (base, uncased) cross-attention model over the top-k retrieved passages, producing span start/end scores plus a passage selection score used as reranker.
quotes: ["The passage selection model serves as a reranker through crossattention between the question and the passage. Although cross-attention is not feasible for retrieving relevant passages in a large corpus due to its nondecomposable nature, it has more capacity than the dual-encoder model sim(q, p)"]
assessment_note: Quote supports cross-attention reranking but omits BERT/span extraction.

text: DrQA reports SQuAD single-model results (70.0 EM / 79.0 F1 test) and open-domain results on SQuAD, TREC, WQ, WikiMovies using a 2016-12-21 Wikipedia dump and distant supervision. Differences in datasets, corpus version and metrics from DPR mean scores are not directly comparable.
quotes: ["The single model trained only on SQuAD is outperformed on all four of the datasets by the multitask model that uses distant supervision."]
assessment_note: Comparison caveat correct; quote covers training variation only.

text: DPR reports end-to-end exact match on NQ, TriviaQA, WQ, TREC, SQuAD using a Dec. 20, 2018 Wikipedia dump, 100-word passages and trained readers; not directly comparable to DrQA's scores due to different corpus, datasets and setup.
quotes: ["we use the English Wikipedia dump from Dec. 20, 2018 as the source documents for answering questions."]
assessment_note: Corpus date quoted; other comparison conditions need evidence.

text: SciBERT is pretrained from scratch/BERT-Base initialization on scientific text: a random sample of 1.14M papers from Semantic Scholar (18% CS, 82% broad biomedical), full text, 3.17B tokens, with an in-domain 30K-piece SciVocab.
quotes: ["We train S CI B ERT on a random sample of 1.14M papers from Semantic Scholar (Ammar et al., 2018). This corpus consists of 18% papers from the computer science domain and 82% from the broad biomedical domain. We use the full text of the papers, not just the abstracts."]
assessment_note: Scientific text and corpus sampling supported.

text: SPECTER does not build its own language-model corpus; it is initialized from the pretrained SciBERT weights (so inherits SciBERT's scientific corpus) and continues training on title-plus-abstract paper input, with the citation graph as additional training data.
quotes: ["We initialize the model from SciBERT pretrained weights (Beltagy et al., 2019) since it is the stateof-the-art pretrained language model on scientific text.", "We use SciBERT as our model initialization as it is optimized for scientific text, though our formulation is general and any Transformer language model instead of SciBERT."]
assessment_note: SciBERT initialization directly supported; extra corpus details need evidence.

text: Standard BERT self-supervised objectives (masked token prediction and next-sentence prediction) on scientific text; no inter-document or citation signal is used.
quotes: ["S CI B ERT follows the same architecture as B ERT but is instead pretrained on scientific text."]
assessment_note: Correct objectives; excerpt mentions architecture but does not identify the objectives.

text: Citation graph as document-level relatedness supervision: a triplet margin loss over (query, cited positive, negative) paper triples, with random negatives plus harder "hard negatives" drawn from citations-of-citations; ablations show this signal is critical.
quotes: ["each training instance is a triplet of papers: a query paper P Q , a positive paper P + and a negative paper P − . The positive paper is a paper that the query paper cites, and the negative paper is a paper that is not cited by the query paper"]
assessment_note: Citation triplet construction directly supported.

text: Missing: the SciBERT paper describes only token-level contextual representations and task fine-tuning; the read passages contain no statement about whether citation information is needed at inference, so no citation requirement is established (inference is on individual sentences/documents without citation context in its tasks).
assessment_note: System marks the cell missing, while the reference expects no citation graph for ordinary encoding.

text: No citation information is needed at inference time; only the title and abstract of the input paper are required, which enables embedding of new papers that have not yet been cited.
quotes: ["Unlike many prior works, at inference time, our model does not require any citation information. This is critical for embedding new papers that have not yet been cited."]
assessment_note: No citation input directly supported.

text: Not comparable as headline numbers: SciBERT reports macro F1 / LAS / UAS on token-, sentence- and span-level tasks (NER, REL, CLS, PICO, DEP) after fine-tuning, averaged over seeds; none of these metrics are nDCG/MAP document-retrieval scores. Overlap exists only where SPECTER uses SciBERT as a baseline.
quotes: ["Keeping with past work, we report macro F1 scores for NER (span-level), macro F1 scores for REL and CLS (sentence-level), and macro F1 for PICO (token-level), and micro F1 for ChemProt specifically. For DEP, we report labeled (LAS) and unlabeled (UAS) attachment scores"]
assessment_note: Correctly flags the shared baseline; local metrics alone do not prove cross-study comparability.

text: Not directly comparable: SPECTER reports document-level SciDocs metrics (F1 classification, MAP/nDCG retrieval, P@1) from frozen, L2-normalized embeddings without task-specific fine-tuning, on a benchmark introduced in this paper; SciBERT's own paper reports no scores on these tasks. Differences also come from setting (fixed embeddings vs fine-tuned task models) and minimal SPECTER tuning versus extensive baseline tuning.
quotes: ["Table 3: Comparison with task-specific fine-tuning. (a) S PECTER (b) SciBERT Figure 2: t-SNE visualization of paper embeddings and their corresponding MAG topics.", "We perform minimal tuning of our model’s hyperparameters based on the performance on the validation set, while baselines are extensively tuned."]
assessment_note: Correct caveat about headline scores, but fails to explain valid same-task comparisons within SciDocs Table 1.

text: General-domain encyclopedic fact verification: claims are verified against the introductory sections of Wikipedia pages, built from a June 2017 Wikipedia dump and sampled from ~50,000 popular pages.
quotes: ["It consists of 185,445 claims generated by altering sentences extracted from Wikipedia and subsequently verified without knowledge of the sentence they were derived from.", "We used the June 2017 Wikipedia dump, processed it with Stanford CoreNLP (Manning et al., 2014), and sampled sentences from the introductory sections of approximately 50,000 popular pages."]
assessment_note: Wikipedia domain directly supported.

text: Specialized scientific/biomedical domain: claims about scientific findings, verified against abstracts from well-regarded journals (Cell, Nature, JAMA, BMJ), drawn from S2ORC and covering diverse biomedical topics; includes a COVID-19 case study against CORD-19.
quotes: ["we randomly sample articles from a manually curated collection of wellregarded journals spanning domains from basic science (e.g., Cell, Nature) to clinical medicine (e.g., JAMA, BMJ)", "indicate that S CI FACT will provide a challenging testbed for the development of new systems designed to retrieve and reason over corpora containing specialized domain knowledge."]
assessment_note: Scientific domain directly supported.

text: Two-stage human construction: annotators wrote claims from randomly sampled Wikipedia sentences (single piece of information about the page entity), then claims were mutated (paraphrase, negation, entity/relation substitution, generalization/specialization), yielding mean length 9.4 tokens.
quotes: ["by human annotators extracting claims from Wikipedia and mutating them in a variety of ways, some of which were meaning-altering.", "specified six types of mutation: paraphrasing, negation, substitution of an entity/relation with a similar/dissimilar one, and making the claim more general/specific.", "The annotators were given a sentence from the sample chosen at random, and were asked to generate a set of claims containing a single piece of information"]
assessment_note: Human construction and mutations directly supported.

text: Claims are expert-written reformulations of naturally occurring citation sentences (citances) from citing papers, into 'atomic scientific claims' without sight of the cited abstract; REFUTES examples were created by an NLP expert writing negations.
quotes: ["we develop a novel annotation protocol in which annotators re-formulate naturally occurring claims in the scientific literature – citation sentences – into atomic scientific claims", "in natural claims because the annotator does not see the cited article’s abstract – the cited abstract – at the time of claim writing.", "To obtain examples where an abstract R EFUTES a claim, an NLP expert wrote negations of existing claims, taking precautions not to bias the negations by using obvious keywords like “not”"]
assessment_note: Citance reformulation and expert negation supported.

text: Evidence is a set of sentences (potentially spanning multiple Wikipedia pages) that jointly justify SUPPORTED/REFUTED labels; NOT ENOUGH INFO claims have no annotated evidence; evidence F1 is computed over predicted sentence sets, with 17.47% F1 reported for the full pipeline.
quotes: ["For the first two classes, the annotators also recorded the sentence(s) forming the necessary evidence for their judgment.", "As in Fig. 1, some claims require multihop inference involving sentences from more than one document to be correctly supported as S UP PORTED /R EFUTED . In this case all sentences must be selected for the evidence to be marked as correct.", "resulting F1 score is 17.47%."]
assessment_note: Wikipedia sentence evidence supported.

text: Evidence is a rationale: up to three mutually exclusive, mostly contiguous sentences within a single cited abstract (28 rationales non-contiguous), labeled at abstract level as SUPPORTS/REFUTES/NO INFO; 63% of cited abstracts contain evidence.
quotes: ["Annotators are shown a single claim - cited abstract pair, and asked to label the pair as S UPPORTS, R EFUTES, or N O I NFO.", "claim, and all rationales consist of at most three sentences. Rationales in S CI FACT are mutually exclusive. 28 rationales contain non-contiguous sentences.", "Overall, the annotators found evidence in 63% of cited abstracts."]
assessment_note: Sentence-level abstract rationales supported.

text: FEVER scores are label accuracy reported both with and without evidence, plus evidence sentence F1; the best system reaches 31.87% when evidence must be correct versus 50.91% ignoring evidence. These figures are not comparable to SCIFACT numbers because the evidence retrieval setting differs: FEVER requires open retrieval over ~50,000 Wikipedia pages, where the document retrieval component often fails (58.27% of analyzed errors) and a much larger, automatically altered claim pool is used.
quotes: ["The best accuracy we achieve on labeling a claim accompanied by the correct evidence is 31.87%, while if we ignore the evidence we achieve 50.91%.", "The information retrieval component of the pipeline failed to identify any correct evidence in 58.27% (n = 560) of cases which accounted for the large disparity between accuracy of the system when evidence was and was not considered."]
assessment_note: Correct caveat; attached quotes cover FEVER's local setting.

text: SCIFACT scores are reported under distinct settings (Oracle abstract, Oracle rationale, Open; abstract-level label F1 and sentence-level rationale P/R/F1), and the paper itself flags that oracle-abstract F1 only 'roughly' matches label accuracy. Conditions differ from FEVER: a small 1,409-claim set over 5,183 abstracts, claims/abstracts often already linked by citations, and top-k=3 retrieval, so its numbers cannot be placed on the same scale as FEVER's open-Wikipedia results; the only shared design element is that FEVER is used as out-of-domain pretraining data.
quotes: ["In the oracle abstract setting, the abstract-level F1 scores are roughly comparable to label classification accuracies", "The S CI FACT dataset consists of 1,409 scientific claims3 verified against a corpus of 5,183 abstracts.", "For the A B STRACT R ETRIEVAL module, the best dev set fullpipeline performance was achieved by retrieving the top k = 3 documents."]
assessment_note: Correct caveat; excerpts cover part of the local protocol.
